title: Starting work
tomorrow: pray at set times or anytime? which does the Church pick?

lines: DO ALL TO THE GLORY OF GOD.
cards: Trays to wipe, boxes to fold, a mop leaning on the wall. Nobody posts their first hour of work. But Paul wrote a line that says even that hour can be holy, and the odd thing is where he put it.
In the Douay-Rheims: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." The glory of God. And he starts with lunch.

teach.b: So why open with eating and drinking? Read the chapter around it and the answer is almost funny.
Paul is answering a practical question from the church in Corinth: is it all right to eat meat that came from a pagan temple, say at a friend's dinner? He works through it case by case.
Then he pulls the lens all the way back: whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do. The plainest thing on the list is the one he names first. If a meal can be offered, so can anything.
He says it again to the Colossians: "All whatsoever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ." In word or in work. The monks took that literally.
The Rule of Saint Benedict calls idleness the enemy of the soul and sets hours for work and hours for holy reading inside the same day, one after the other. So offered work isn't a different job.
It's the same tray, the same inbox, with one thing added at the start: whom it's for.
And the start is the easy place to add it, before the rest of the day crowds in. One to tell a friend: Paul's great line about the glory of God comes out of an argument about what to eat at dinner.

how: Many Catholics begin the workday with a short offering of their work to God, and monasteries following the Rule of Saint Benedict set hours for work and prayer side by side.

o: a blessing a priest gives a new business
beginning the day's work by offering it to God
the very first day at a brand-new job

games.q: where the line comes from — tap the pairs.

s: Paul's 'do all to the glory of God' comes in a passage about food
he's answering whether to eat temple meat at a friend's dinner.
the Rule of Benedict tells monks to pray instead of work
it calls idleness the enemy of the soul and sets hours for both.
offering work means thinking about God every second of it
the offering is made at the start: whom the work is for.

games.q: your cousin starts at a warehouse: eight hours of scanning boxes. he says nothing about it could be for God. by Paul's line, what's true?
o: the scanning itself can be offered, starting with the first box.
he should find meaningful work first; scanning can't glorify anyone.
only his breaks count, if he prays during them.
games.why: Paul starts with eating and drinking, then says whatsoever else you do. the plain task is exactly what can be offered.

practice: Name the very first task waiting for you tomorrow, the plainest one. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if you were holding it.
Offer it there, with Paul's words, do all to the glory of God, or with the plain intention to do it well for someone.

wordCard.voice: Starting work. The first task of the day, handed over before the rest begin.

orig.note: Greek: to the glory of God, the end of Paul's line in 1 Corinthians 10:31.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: offered work, the same tray or inbox with one thing added. That's today.
